title: C1019 — Inline connector reference
introduction:
I read this inline connector reference by choosing the harness and connector gender first, then following the drawing’s cavity labels into the matching table. Think of the cavity as a street address and the circuit as the occupant: matching housing shapes alone does not tell you which signal lives there.

The function entries concern cylinder head temperature sensing and powertrain signal returns. The drawings show different left-to-right cavity arrangements, so read each face independently. This guide explains the reference; access, physical viewing direction, electrical testing, wire selection and replacement require information beyond this sheet. Gauge conventions and the Size and Used codes are not defined here. Conflicting male-face assignments remain unresolved below. The summary Pin Count differs from the cavity count on each individual face; whether it counts across both faces is unexplained.

edits.why: I start with the harness identity, then use the adjacent Gender and Fpn entries to distinguish this face from its counterpart. The housing outline helps compare the printed drawings, but its projections do not establish a release mechanism or a physical viewing direction.

Find the printed cavity label in the Cavity column, then read across the same row. Circuit Number identifies the electrical circuit; Color and Gauge describe the listed lead; Function explains its role; Terminal Part Number identifies the listed terminal. Here, repeated cavity entries associate different functions with the same location, and the blank Qualifier cells do not explain which applies. Keep those entries separate rather than turning them into a definitive wiring assignment.

I use this face’s own printed labels and identification table. The cavity labels reverse their left-to-right positions relative to the other drawing, so carrying a position across by eye can send you to the wrong entry. This comparison describes the page illustrations, not a confirmed wire-side or mating-side viewing instruction.

Read each cavity’s complete row to distinguish the cylinder head temperature sensor circuit from the powertrain signal return. The return entry retains its parenthetical identifying labels; do not silently substitute the differently identified return from the other face. N/A in Terminal Part Number leaves no terminal identifier to retrieve from these rows.

I compare Engineering Shell with Fpn in the chosen face’s identification table, then read Number and Service Part from that same pigtail row. This keeps the kit associated with its listed shell instead of treating the catalog as a lucky dip. Gauge, Material and Cavities describe the listed kit; they are not installation instructions or permission to select replacement wire. The Image entries are filenames, not additional kit illustrations shown here.
This regional entry supplies a Product Id without a shell or connector-face cross-reference. I keep it as a separate catalog reference rather than assigning it to either face.

originalAuthorHold: The male-face table assigns both the temperature-sensor circuit and the signal-return circuit to each cavity, with blank qualifiers. The supplied evidence does not identify the applicable configuration or establish a unique male-face assignment.
The summary Pin Count is 4, while each face drawing shows cavities 1 and 2. Whether the summary counts across both faces is unexplained; it cannot be treated as a per-face cavity count.

editorialRevision.scope: Complete independent active-agent review of all 45 primary units, three complete source pages and both figures, and 6 edits. Summary count and overlapping male-face assignment ambiguity retained for bounded identification reading only.
